chapter_theme: The false renunciant, whose outward form hides an unrenounced heart, is exposed through a run of precise images. The chapter insists that conduct, not appearance, is the test, and ends by declaring the outward marks of renunciation unnecessary.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the fault of such conduct (271-275), the fault of its practitioners and the need to recognize and avoid them (276-278), how to recognize them (279), and the excellence of those free of it (280).

271.reading: The five elements laugh inwardly at the concealed conduct of one with a deceitful mind.
271.nuance: A hypocrite can't escape witnesses, because his own body is one of them. Parimelazhagar identifies the hidden conduct as sexual, and he carries this through 273 and 274, but the verse doesn't specify.

positions.position: The elements themselves are the cosmic witnesses, mingled in his body and laughing without his knowing.
positions.quote: உடம்பாய் அவனோடு கலந்து நிற்கின்ற பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் கண்டு தம்முள்ளே நகும்.

positions.position: 'Elements' stands for the senses, their products, which know what he does.

272.reading: What will an appearance as high as the sky do, if one's own heart sinks into a fault one knows to be a fault?
272.nuance: தான்அறி, 'that one knows', is the crux. Parimelazhagar's point is that a fault done unknowingly can be washed away, but one done knowingly can't, so the outward habit only frightens others.

273.reading: A person without strength taking on the form of the strong is like a cow grazing wrapped in a tiger's skin.
273.nuance: Parimelazhagar presses the image hard. The guards don't chase the 'tiger' because tigers don't eat grass, and because they are afraid, and the cow leaves its own grass for another's crop. So the renouncer leaves his wife and pursues other men's. The strength lacking is mastery of one's own mind; the rest is his extrapolation.

274.reading: Hiding in austerity and doing what isn't austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush and snaring birds.
274.nuance: With 273 this gives two opposed animals: the cow is harmless inside a predator's skin, and the hunter is a predator behind harmless leaves. The hypocrite is both, weak before his desire and dangerous to others. That pairing is my own observation. Manakkudavar gives Arjuna as an example.

275.reading: The hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many evils, with cries of 'what, what!'
275.nuance: என்பார், 'those who say', quietly marks the claim as words only, and Parimelazhagar says that the attachment was only cut in speech.

positions.position: The cry belongs to the hypocrites, who later lament what they have done.
positions.quote: பின் 'என் செய்தோம்! என் செய்தோம்! என்று தாமே இரங்கும்வகை,

positions.position: The cry belongs to everyone, who exclaim at such a person, and எற்று is a regional word.

276.reading: None are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced in heart, live by deceiving as though they had renounced.
276.nuance: Why is deceit the height of cruelty? Parimelazhagar has a remarkable answer: the victims are donors, whose gifts to the unworthy earn them a low birth, so the fraud returns harm for help. He supports this from the Civakacintamani, not from the verse.

positions.position: They harm those who feed them, since gifts to the unrestrained bring donors a low birth.
positions.quote: தமக்கு ஆவன செய்தார்க்கு ஆகாதன விளைத்தலின் 'வன்கணார் இல்' என்றார்.

277.reading: The world holds those who, though looking outwardly like the red kunri seed, are inwardly black as its tip.
277.nuance: The kunri is a closely observed choice, since its red and black belong to a single small seed. உடைத்து, 'it holds', says only that such people exist. Manakkudavar takes this as a warning to the wise not to judge ascetics by form.

278.reading: Many people, with impurity in their minds, bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed.
278.nuance: பலர், 'many', comes right after the 'some' of 277 and is a social observation. Water cleans what isn't dirty and leaves what is. Parimelazhagar specifies the impurity as desire, anger and delusion.

positions.position: They literally bathe, to appear distinguished by austerity, and hide behind this.
positions.quote: பிறர்க்குத் தவத்தான் மாட்சிமையுடையராய் நீரின் மூழ்கிக் காட்டி;

positions.position: நீராடி isn't bathing: they put on the நீர்மை, the nature, of the distinguished.
Water is an analogy: they hide under the name of greatness as a diver hides under water.
positions.quote: நீருக்குள் மூழ்கியோர் தம்மை மறைத்துக் கொள்வது போல,

279.reading: The arrow is cruel and the curved lute is straight, so know people by the nature of their deeds.
279.nuance: The verse makes shape deceive in both directions: the straight kills and the curved delights. It does more than warn that some who look good are bad, since it also suggests that some who look wrong are good.

280.reading: Neither shaving nor long hair is needed, if one gives up what the world condemns.
280.nuance: The test of renunciation is set by what the ordinary world condemns, and not by a special ascetic code. Parimelazhagar narrows உலகம் to the high-minded, but Manakkudavar leaves it as people generally. The verse removes the outward marks, not renunciation itself.

links.note: Both make one's own heart the witness: 272 says that an outward show can't help when the heart knows the fault, and 293 says the heart will burn the one who lies against what it knows. Self-knowledge is the Kural's court of last resort.
278's மனத்தது மாசாக is the exact opposite of 34's மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன். 34 states the principle that all else is show, and 278 gives the social picture of the show in practice.

827 warns that a bowing enemy's words are like a bow's bend, which signals harm. 279 says the lute's curve is straight and the arrow's straightness is cruel. So the curve is a warning in one verse and no evidence at all in the other, which supports 279's point that shape can't be read directly.

The same utterance appears in both: in 88, the miser who fed no guests later says பற்றற்றேம் as a lament for lost support, and in 275 the hypocrite says it as a boast of non-attachment. Both are words that the speaker's life makes hollow.

source_issues: 277: the verse text has முக்கிற், where the commentators read மூக்கின் or மூக்கு.
278: Manakkudavar's entry has an empty (எ - று) marker, which doesn't affect the sense.
